title.en: Logging: Print Statements That Grow Up

description.en: print() is great for a first look, but it can't be turned down, filtered, or left in safely. Learn Python's logging module: levels, named loggers, one-line configuration, and why logs beat scattered prints once a program is bigger than a page.

story_variants.en:
## Print, But With a Volume Knob

You already know `print()` debugging: drop a line in, see the real value, move on. It works. The trouble starts when you *keep* those lines. Ship them and your users see noise; delete them and the next bug sends you back to re-type them.

Python's built-in `logging` module is `print` with three upgrades: every message has a **severity level**, you can **turn the volume** up or down in one place, and you can say **where** the messages go (screen, file, anywhere) without touching the code that produces them.

> **Key idea:** Write log calls once, at the right level. Decide *later*, with one setting, how much of it you want to see.

## The five levels

| Level | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `DEBUG` | Fine detail you only want while hunting a bug ("adding 5") |
| `INFO` | Normal milestones ("order 7 received") |
| `WARNING` | Something odd but survivable ("stock low") |
| `ERROR` | An operation failed |
| `CRITICAL` | The program may not continue |

Setting `level=logging.INFO` means: show INFO and everything more severe, hide DEBUG. Flip it to `DEBUG` when you are investigating, back to `INFO` when you are done. No code edits, no forgotten prints.

## Setting it up

```python
import logging, sys
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(levelname)s:%(name)s:%(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("orders")
log.info("order 7 received")
```

`getLogger("orders")` gives you a **named logger**, so in a big program you can tell *which part* spoke. The `format` string chooses what each line shows; real programs usually add `%(asctime)s` for a timestamp (we leave it out here so the output is always identical).

## Why not just print?

- **Filtering:** hide the chatty DEBUG lines in production, show them in a bug hunt.
- **Context for free:** level, logger name, time, even file and line number via the format string.
- **Tracebacks:** `log.exception("payment failed")` inside an `except` block records the message *and* the full traceback.
- **Destinations:** the same call can write to the console, a file, or a log service.

## Honest caveats

- `basicConfig` only takes effect the first time (unless you pass `force=True`, as we do here so lessons re-run cleanly).
- Prefer `log.info("x=%s", x)` over an f-string in hot code: the `%s` form skips the formatting work if the level is hidden. For learning, f-strings are fine.
- Never log secrets (passwords, tokens). Logs get copied around.

## Where it fits in the track

Use `print` for the quick first look, a **log** for anything you want to keep, and a **test** (next lesson) for anything you never want to break again.

left.label: print() everywhere: can't be silenced, mixed into real output, deleted and re-typed for every bug

right.label: logging: one call per event, filtered by level from a single setting

description.en: Both report the same facts. With logging you decide how much to see by changing one level, instead of editing every line.

animation_sequence.code:
import logging, sys
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(levelname)s:%(name)s:%(message)s", force=True)
log = logging.getLogger("orders")
log.debug("raw payload: {...}")
log.info("order 7 received")
log.warning("stock low for sku A1")

executionSteps.description: DEBUG message is below the INFO threshold, so nothing is printed. Same call, hidden by one setting.
INFO passes the threshold and prints with the format we chose.
WARNING is more severe than INFO, so it shows too.

instruction.en:
Add logging to total(). Skip negative prices with a WARNING 'skipping negative price

' (and continue), log a DEBUG 'adding

' for each accepted price, and finish with an INFO 'total='. The logger is set to INFO, so the DEBUG lines stay hidden. Expected output: WARNING:skipping negative price -2 INFO:total=12

practice_challenges.starter_code:
import logging, sys logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s:%(message)s", force=True) log = logging.getLogger("shop") def total(prices): s = 0 for p in prices: # TODO 1: if p is negative, log a WARNING "skipping negative price

" and continue # TODO 2: log a DEBUG "adding

" (it stays hidden at INFO level - that is the point!) s += p # TODO 3: log an INFO "total=" return s total([5, -2, 7])

en: Each TODO is one call on the logger `log`: log.warning(...), log.debug(...), log.info(...).
For the negative case use `continue` after the warning so the price is not added.
The DEBUG line produces no output at INFO level - that is expected.

practice_challenges.test_code:
import logging
logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)
assert total([1, 2]) == 3
assert total([4, -1]) == 4
assert total([]) == 0

Why is logging usually better than leaving print() calls in shipped code?

en: You can filter or redirect it with one setting instead of editing every line

under_the_hood.summary: logging.getLogger(name) returns a cached logger in a dotted-name tree; each call first compares its level with the logger's effective level, creates a LogRecord only if enabled, and passes it to handlers on the logger and its ancestors.

steps.title: Loggers form a tree by name
steps.body: `logging.getLogger('orders')` returns the same object every time you ask for 'orders', from a dict kept by the logging manager. Names with dots form a hierarchy: 'orders.payments' is a child of 'orders', which is a child of the root logger.

steps.title: The level check comes first
steps.body: `log.debug('raw payload: ...')` checks `isEnabledFor(DEBUG)`. The logger has no level of its own, so it uses the nearest ancestor's: the root was set to INFO by basicConfig. DEBUG (10) is below INFO (20), so the call returns immediately and no record is built.

steps.title: Records are built lazily
steps.body: For `log.info('order %s received', order_id)` that passes the check, logging creates a LogRecord with the message template, the args, time, logger name, file and line. The `%` formatting happens later, only when a handler formats the record. So pass arguments separately instead of building an f-string that is wasted when the level is off.

steps.title: Handlers write the output
steps.body: The record is passed to every handler on the logger, then to handlers on each ancestor (propagation) up to the root. basicConfig added one StreamHandler to the root with the format `%(levelname)s:%(name)s:%(message)s`, so the output line is `INFO:orders:order 7 received`.

steps.title: One switch changes the volume
steps.body: Because filtering happens by level in the logger and handlers, changing `level=logging.DEBUG` in one place reveals every debug line without editing the code that logs. Handlers can also send records to files or other destinations.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Log calls are cheap when filtered out, because the level check happens before any work. Name loggers by module, pass arguments lazily, and control what you see in one configuration spot.
